general.who_this_is_for: The organization's own authorized people (for example a board officer). Helpers can explain these steps; they never file recovery requests, contact providers, or try to log in on the organization's behalf.
before_you_start: Decide who has authority to recover the account (usually a board decision; write it down in the minutes).
Pick ONE person to do the recovery so the provider sees a single, consistent request.
Do not guess passwords or answers repeatedly: failed attempts can lock the account for longer, or permanently.
Use the provider's official help site only. Ignore anyone who contacts you offering to recover the account; that is a common scam.
If the domain or website is redirecting somewhere strange, recover the domain (registrar) account first: it controls where the website and email go.
proof_checklist: The organization's legal name, exactly as registered (and EIN or charity number if it has one).
Formation or registration documents (for example articles of incorporation) and, if applicable, the tax-exemption determination letter.
A letter on the organization's letterhead, signed by an officer, naming who is authorized to recover the account.
Government photo ID of that authorized person (providers usually ask for this; share it only through the provider's official upload process).
Billing evidence: invoices, receipt numbers, the last digits of the card or bank account used, and approximate payment dates.
Account details you still know: the account email or username, customer number, domain names, page or site names, and when it was created.
The email address or phone number that used to be on the account, even if nobody can access it anymore.
expired_domain: Act immediately: many registrars keep an expired domain for a renewal grace period, followed by a redemption period (often around 30 days) with a higher fee. After that it can be released and bought by anyone.
Check the registrar's own terms for its exact periods and fees.
If the registrar is unresponsive or refuses to follow its published policies, ICANN Contractual Compliance accepts complaints about registrars of generic domains (.org, .com, .net and others).
after_recovery: Turn on two-step login (2FA) with an authenticator app or security key, not just text messages if you can avoid it.
Add a second administrator who is a current board member or staff, so one person leaving can never lock the organization out again.
Update the recovery email and phone to role-based ones the organization controls (for example an admin@ mailbox), not a personal address.
Turn on auto-renew for domains and confirm the payment method is current.
Remove anyone who no longer needs access (see access_offboarding) and record the account in org_registers.
what_helpers_never_do: File recovery requests, contact the provider, or log in on the organization's behalf.
Ask for, store, or handle the organization's passwords, recovery codes, or ID documents.
Use tricks, impersonation, or third-party 'recovery services'.

godaddy.name: GoDaddy (domains and hosting)
godaddy.notes: Registrars usually verify ownership with ID and billing details. If a former volunteer's personal account holds the domain, ask about a change of account holder or an account-to-account move once they (or proof of the organization's ownership) can be provided.

namecheap.name: Namecheap (domains)
namecheap.notes: Have the domain name, approximate registration date and billing details ready.

squarespace.name: Squarespace (websites and domains)
squarespace.notes: Website ownership and domain ownership can be separate; ask about both. Site contributors cannot take over ownership on their own; the owner role must be transferred.

wix.name: Wix (websites)
wix.notes: If a former volunteer owns the site, a site transfer to an organization account is the usual route.

wordpress_com.name: WordPress.com (websites)
wordpress_com.notes: Self-hosted WordPress is different: access depends on the web host account, so recover that first.

google_workspace.name: Google Workspace (email and documents)
search_terms: verify domain ownership to recover admin access
google_workspace.notes: Admin recovery may involve proving control of the domain (for example by adding a DNS record), so domain access often comes first.

microsoft_365.name: Microsoft 365 (email and documents)
microsoft_365.notes: Organizations with Microsoft nonprofit offers may also have a partner or reseller who can help; check billing records.

facebook_page.name: Facebook Page
facebook_page.notes: Pages are managed through people's personal profiles. Any remaining admin can add new ones; if none remain, use the official help forms only.

instagram.name: Instagram
search_terms: lost access to email or phone
instagram.notes: If linked to a Facebook Page or Meta business account, recovering that may restore Instagram access.

registrar_other.name: Any other domain registrar
search_terms: look up the domain to find its registrar, then use that registrar's own support site
registrar_other.notes: Use domain_research rdap <domain> or the ICANN lookup to see which registrar holds the domain. If a registrar does not follow its published policies, ICANN Contractual Compliance (https://www.icann.org/compliance) accepts complaints for generic domains.
